title: Cell-free reconstitution of peroxisomal matrix protein import using Xenopus egg extract
author: Skowyra, Rapoport

The fluorescent cargo (GFP-SKL) will be added later, after warming up the extract.Note: Dilute the purified PEX5 and GFP-SKL to the indicated 20× stock concentrations using cold XBHS buffer and keep on ice.Note: PEX5 may be used at higher concentrations (≤ 1 μM) to accelerate import,1 but the recommended concentration is sufficient and close to the concentration of endogenous PEX5 (∼50 nM).54 Higher concentrations of GFP-SKL are not recommended because they will increase the background and reduce the visibility of GFP-SKL imported into peroxisomes.Note: Egg extract is very viscous. steps.title: Obtain approvals and prime frogs
steps.instruction: Arrange institutional permissions for housing, handling, and ovulating Xenopus laevis frogs; prime each frog with 200 U pregnant‑mare‑serum gonadotropin (PMSG) injected into the dorsal lymph sac using a 27‑gauge needle and sterile 1 mL syringe; keep primed frogs at 16 °C in ≥4 L of reverse‑osmosis‑purified, rock‑salt‑conditioned water per frog; if allowed, fast frogs during priming to improve egg quality.

steps.title: Inject frogs with PMSG
steps.instruction: Using a fine 27‑gauge hypodermic needle and sterile 1‑mL syringe, inject 200 U PMSG into the dorsal lymph sac of each frog; discard used needles in a sharps container; maintain injected frogs at 16 °C in conditioned water (≥4 L per frog).

steps.title: Collect eggs and dejelly
steps.instruction: The morning after injection, transfer frogs to a new container with ≥4 L conditioned water per frog and allow ovulation for ~24 h at 16 °C; collect the laid eggs into a shallow glass dish; discard any stringy, deformed, or white‑puffy eggs; dejelly by adding one‑third of the dejellying solution (MMR buffer with 20 g L⁻¹ cysteine, pH 7.5–8) at a time, swirling gently for 1–2 min per addition; repeat three times, then swirl for 10–15 min until jelly coats are removed (≤ 25 min total); decant most buffer after each step; add 200 µL XBS buffer, swirl 2 min, repeat three more times, finishing with a final 200 µL XBS addition.

steps.title: Prepare required buffers
steps.instruction: Prepare the following buffers fresh as indicated:

substeps.instruction: Lysis buffer (1 L): 50 mM Tris (pH 7.5, 1 M stock), 150 mM NaCl (2 M stock), 1 mM EDTA (0.5 M stock), water to 1 L; adjust pH to 7.5 at RT (8.0 at 4 °C), chill to 4 °C; store ≤ 1 yr.
High‑salt lysis buffer (1 L): 50 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 600 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, water to 1 L; adjust pH as above; chill; store ≤ 1 yr.
Elution buffer (40 mL): 50 mM Tris (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 40 mM reduced glutathione, water to 40 mL; adjust pH to 7.5 at RT; prepare just before use, do not store.

XBHS buffer (1 L): 1× XB buffer (20× stock: 50 mM Tris, 250 mM sucrose, 30 mM HEPES, pH 7.8), plus additional 30 mM HEPES to reach 40 mM total; adjust pH to 7.8 with KOH; sterile‑filter; store ≤ 1 yr at 4 °C.
Dejellying solution (MMR buffer, 1 L): 50 mM sucrose, 20 g L⁻¹ cysteine, adjust pH 7.5–8 with NaOH; prepare fresh, do not store.

steps.title: Purify recombinant PEX5
steps.instruction: Express and purify wild‑type X. laevis PEX5 (short isoform) as an N‑terminal GST fusion, then remove the GST tag with 3C protease.

substeps.instruction: Transform E. coli BL21 Rosetta 2(DE3) with plasmid pMSV‑013; select on chloramphenicol + kanamycin.
Grow 2 L culture in 2×YT at 37 °C (use 1 L medium per 2‑L baffled flask) with antibiotics to OD ≈ 0.6.
Induce with 1 mM IPTG (from 1 M stock) and incubate 16–20 h at 16 °C.
Harvest cells at 4 000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C; decant supernatant.
Resuspend pellet in 50 mL cold lysis buffer per liter of culture; pool to ~100 mL.
Add DTT to 1 mM (1 M stock) and protease‑inhibitor tablets; keep cold.
Lyse by high‑pressure homogenization (e.g., EmulsiFlex‑C3) with cooling jacket; alternatively sonicate.
Add PMSF to 1 mM (1 M stock) post‑lysis.
Centrifuge lysate ≥ 30 000 × g for 30 min at 4 °C; collect supernatant.
Incubate clarified lysate with 2–3 mL glutathione‑agarose beads (equilibrated in lysis buffer) for 30 min at RT with agitation (do not exceed 30 min).
Collect beads on a 20‑mL gravity column, discard lysate.
Wash beads sequentially with 50 mL cold lysis buffer, 50 mL cold high‑salt lysis buffer, and 50 mL cold lysis buffer; add DTT to 1 mM just before each wash.
Resuspend beads in 5 mL cold lysis buffer; keep on ice; add DTT to 1 mM.
Elute overnight (16–20 h) at 4 °C with 1 µM GST‑tagged 3C protease in the bead suspension.
Drain beads, wash with 4–6 mL lysis buffer, pool wash with flow‑through.
Concentrate pooled flow‑through to ~0.5 mL using a 10‑kDa centrifugal concentrator; centrifuge 20 000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C to pellet aggregates.
Gel‑filter supernatant on a Superdex 200 10/300 GL column in XBHS buffer (supplemented with 1 mM DTT) at 4 °C; collect the major peak (~11.5 mL).
Pool peak fractions and concentrate to 100 µM (using 10‑kDa concentrator); calculate concentration using ε = 93 390 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, MW = 65 kDa; expect 100–200 µL.
Aliquot 5 µL portions into 0.2‑mL PCR tubes, snap‑freeze in liquid N₂, store at –80 °C; avoid refreezing.

steps.title: Purify recombinant GFP‑SKL
steps.instruction: Express and purify GFP‑SKL (GST‑fusion, tag removed) as a fluorescent cargo.

substeps.instruction: Transform E. coli BL21 Rosetta 2(DE3) with plasmid pMSV‑064; select as above.
Express and purify using the same protocol as for PEX5 (steps up to bead binding).
Gel‑filter the protein on a Superdex 75 10/300 GL column in XBHS buffer; major peak at ~11.5 mL.
Pool peak fractions and concentrate to 100 µM (ε = 21 890 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, MW = 27 kDa); expect ~200 µL.
Aliquot 5 µL into 0.2‑mL PCR tubes, snap‑freeze in liquid N₂, store at –80 °C.

steps.title: Purify GST‑PEX14 binding domain
steps.instruction: Express and purify the GST‑tagged PEX5‑binding domain (aa 19‑78) of X. laevis PEX14.

substeps.instruction: Transform E. coli BL21 Rosetta 2(DE3) with plasmid pMSV‑099; select as above.
Grow 4 L culture as for PEX5; harvest and lyse as above.
Bind lysate to 10 mL glutathione‑agarose (using a 50‑mL gravity column); wash with 100 mL buffer per wash step.
Elute with 10 mL elution buffer (cold, containing 1 mM DTT) at RT for 10 min; swirl gently; repeat elution twice more (total ~30 mL).
Pool eluates, concentrate to ~5 mL (10‑kDa concentrator).
Gel‑filter on a Superdex 200 HiLoad 26/600 PG column (or dialyze overnight into XBHS buffer if column unavailable) with 1 mM DTT.
Pool dimer peak (retention 180–190 mL) and concentrate to 300 µM (≈10 mg mL⁻¹) using 10‑kDa concentrator; calculate with ε = 42 860 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹, MW = 33 kDa; expect ~5 mL.
Aliquot 1.5‑mL portions into 2‑mL microfuge tubes, snap‑freeze in liquid N₂, store at –80 °C.

steps.title: Prepare agarose beads for PEX5 depletion
steps.instruction: Couple the GST‑PEX14 binding domain to Affi‑Gel 15 resin and wash to obtain PEX5‑depleting beads.

substeps.instruction: Thaw one 1.5‑mL aliquot of GST‑PEX14 domain (10 mg mL⁻¹); centrifuge 20 000 × g for 20 min at 4 °C; keep supernatant on ice.
Thaw 500 µL Affi‑Gel 15 resin (stored in isopropanol at –80 °C) on ice 5–10 min; invert bottle to mix; transfer to 2‑mL tube on ice using wide‑bore tip.
Let resin settle, aspirate isopropanol, add 1 mL ice‑cold MilliQ water, invert to resuspend; centrifuge 1 500 × g for 1 min at 4 °C; keep on ice.
Wash resin once with ice‑cold water, then three times with 1 mL ice‑cold XBH buffer.
Aspirate all liquid; add 1.5 mL cold purified GST‑PEX14 (10 mg mL⁻¹) to resin; invert to mix; rotate overnight (16–20 h) at 4 °C.
Transfer resin to a clean 10‑mL Poly‑Prep gravity column; wash sequentially with 10 mL cold XBH buffer, 10 mL cold high‑salt XBH, 10 mL cold XBH.
Wash with 4 mL cold glycine buffer (pH 2.4), immediately followed by 10 mL cold XBH (neutralize); repeat glycine wash two more times.
Confirm absence of protein in final flow‑through by Bradford assay.
Resuspend resin in equal volume of XBHS buffer (1:1 suspension); transfer 1.5‑mL aliquots to microfuge tubes; store at 4 °C (stable for months).

steps.title: Passivate coverslips with PEG
steps.instruction: Create PEG‑coated, hydrophilic coverslips to prevent protein adsorption during imaging.

substeps.instruction: Arrange coverslips in a rack; rinse with MilliQ water; blow off excess water with compressed air or rubber bellows; dry on hot plate or in hot oven.
Expose dried coverslips to oxygen plasma for 4 min at 200 W, 0.1 Torr O₂ (500 II plasma etcher parameters).
Prepare PEG solution: weigh 30–40 mg methoxy‑PEG‑silane into 1.5‑mL tube; add 900 µL PEG solvent; heat tube at 80 °C for a few seconds until dissolved; keep at 80 °C.
Pipette 20 µL PEG solution onto center of one coverslip; immediately place a second coverslip on top to form a sandwich; ensure even spreading (bubbles acceptable).
Place sandwich upright in coverslip rack; incubate in oven pre‑warmed to 80 °C overnight (16–20 h).
Next day, remove rack, store coverslips at room temperature in a closed container (e.g., empty pipette‑tip box); usable ≥ 1 month.

steps.title: Generate Xenopus egg extract
steps.instruction: Crush dejellied eggs by centrifugation, isolate the cytoplasmic (interphase) fraction, and lock it with cycloheximide.

substeps.instruction: Transfer packed, dejellied eggs into 5‑mL thin‑walled ultracentrifuge tubes: add 1 mL XBS buffer to each tube, then dispense eggs from a cut‑tip 2‑mL polypropylene pipet into the buffer, filling tube ~≥ ½ full without overfilling.

Aspirate most of the covering buffer; centrifuge at 16 °C, 350 × g for 1 min, then immediately increase to 1 200 × g for another minute (total 2 min) to pack eggs tightly; verify packing by tilting tube (eggs should not slide).
Aspirate residual buffer; add protease‑inhibitor/cytochalasin/cycloheximide 1000× stock (volume calculated to achieve final concentrations as in the stock solution) directly onto packed eggs.
Centrifuge in SW 55 Ti swinging‑bucket rotor at 12 100 × g for 15 min at 16 °C; place tubes on ice.
Identify three layers: top yellow lipid, middle straw‑colored cytoplasm (extract), bottom dark pellet.
Wipe tube exterior with 100 % ethanol‑soaked kimwipe; pierce side of tube just above pellet with an 18‑gauge beveled needle attached to a 1‑mL syringe (bevel up).
Sweep needle side‑to‑side while slowly pulling plunger to aspirate cytoplasmic layer (fill 1‑mL syringe in 40–60 s); expel into a chilled microfuge tube.
Repeat for each tube using a fresh needle/syringe each time.
Add appropriate volume of 1000× stock (protease inhibitors, cytochalasin, cycloheximide) to each extract tube; mix by inversion.
Collect extract at tube bottom using a touch‑spin centrifuge; keep on ice.
If extract appears gray (debris contamination), clarify by centrifuging 5 min at 10 000 × g, 4 °C; transfer supernatant to new tube with wide‑bore tip.
Use extract promptly; discard if kept on ice > 5–6 h.

steps.title: Set up peroxisomal import reactions
steps.instruction: Combine PEX5‑depleted extract, recombinant PEX5 (or controls), and GFP‑SKL to monitor matrix import.

substeps.instruction: Prepare three 0.2‑mL PCR tubes on ice (Reaction 1: +PEX5, Reaction 2: no PEX5, Reaction 3: mock‑depleted/unmanipulated extract).
For each tube add in order (starting with extract):
– 18 µL PEX5‑depleted egg extract (or unmanipulated extract for Reaction 3).
– 1 µL purified recombinant PEX5 in XBHS buffer (2 µM stock) for Reaction 1 only; omit for Reactions 2 and 3.
– 1 µL XBHS buffer (to bring volume to 20 µL before cargo).
Mix gently by flicking; spin briefly on touch‑spin to collect liquid at tube bottom.
Pre‑warm tubes for 5 min at 24 °C in a pre‑heated 96‑well thermoblock or compatible block heater.
After warming, add 1 µL GFP‑SKL (10 µM stock in XBHS) to each tube to achieve 0.5 µM final cargo concentration (20× dilution).
Flick tubes gently, spin briefly on touch‑spin.
Incubate tubes at 24 °C for 1 h in the thermoblock (alternatively 16–18 °C, noting increased viscosity).
After incubation, proceed to imaging; longer incubations (> several h) are discouraged due to apoptosis risk.

steps.title: Quantify import by fluorescence microscopy
steps.instruction: Image the reactions and analyze GFP‑SKL peroxisomal fluorescence using ImageJ as described in the referenced STAR Methods; normalize and compare import levels across the three reactions.

description: Peroxisomes occur in nearly all eukaryotic cells2 and perform important functions related to lipid metabolism3 and redox homeostasis,4 among others.5,6,7 Peroxisomes are vital for human health, as defective import of enzymes into the peroxisomal lumen (matrix) causes severe neurological disorders.8 Without exception, peroxisomes import their matrix proteins from the cytosol.9 Proteins can be imported into peroxisomes in a folded state or even as oligomers,10 which fundamentally differs from protein import into the endoplasmic reticulum or mitochondria.11,12 Understanding how proteins are imported into peroxisomes is thus of considerable therapeutic and scientific interest. Most peroxisomal matrix proteins contain a C-terminal peroxisome targeting signal (PTS) that consists of the amino acid sequence Ser-Lys-Leu (SKL) or variants of it.13 The PTS is recognized in the cytosol by the soluble receptor PEX5.14 PEX5 is recruited to peroxisomes by the membrane proteins PEX13 and PEX14, and then moves the cargo into the matrix.9 PEX5 must then return to the cytosol. This retrieval process requires PEX5 to be ubiquitinated on a conserved cysteine15,16 by the PEX2-PEX10-PEX12 ubiquitin ligase complex17 and extracted into the cytosol by the PEX1-PEX6 AAA ATPase.18 Deubiquitination in the cytosol allows PEX5 to start another round of import.19,20 While this overall pathway of peroxisomal import is well established, the underlying mechanism is poorly understood. In vitro systems have provided invaluable insight into the import mechanism.21,22 One type of import system uses semi-permeabilized cells that are bathed in a cytosolic extract containing reporter cargo and import components.23,24,25 Another uses post-nuclear supernatants or purified peroxisomes prepared from cells26,27 or from tissues such as animal liver28,29 or plant cotyledons.30,31 Post-nuclear supernatants are particularly attractive because they can be easily manipulated or scaled up.28 However, current import sys
